notes.meaning: Amaziah became king of Judah at twenty-five years old and ruled in Jerusalem for twenty-nine years. His mother Jehoaddan was from Jerusalem, showing the royal line remained rooted in the Davidic capital. Part of his reign was later shared alongside his son Uzziah.

Amaziah obeyed God on the outside, but his heart was not fully devoted to the Lord. He started well by keeping God's laws, but he lacked deep, lasting commitment. Doing the right things without full devotion leaves room for trouble later.

Once his rule was secure, Amaziah put to death the royal officials who had assassinated his father, King Joash. Yet he spared their children, deliberately obeying the law of Moses that forbids punishing children for their parents' crimes. He showed real restraint and respect for God's word by refusing the common ancient practice of wiping out entire families.

Amaziah organized the men of Judah and Benjamin by families and appointed commanders over units of thousands and hundreds. He counted all men twenty and older fit for battle, finding three hundred thousand skilled soldiers. This army was far smaller than the forces of earlier kings, showing that recent troubles had weakened the nation.

Feeling his own army was not big enough, Amaziah hired one hundred thousand soldiers from the northern kingdom of Israel for one hundred talents of silver. He looked to military numbers rather than trusting God for victory.

A prophet warned the king not to take the hired northern troops into battle because God was not with the idolatrous kingdom of Israel. The prophet warned with sharp irony that even if Amaziah fought with great courage, God would make him fall if he relied on those allies. God alone has the power to give victory or bring defeat.

Amaziah worried about losing the large payment of silver he had already handed over to Israel's soldiers. The prophet gave the comforting answer that the Lord can easily give him far more than that sum. Obeying God might bring short-term financial loss, but God is able to provide whatever we need.

Amaziah obeyed the prophet and dismissed the northern mercenaries, sending them back home. The hired troops left in a fury because they felt insulted and were cheated out of their share of war plunder.

Amaziah took courage, led his own army to the Valley of Salt south of the Dead Sea, and killed ten thousand Edomite soldiers. Judah's army also took ten thousand captives and threw them from a high cliff to their deaths. While God gave Judah the victory, the king acted with extreme cruelty toward the prisoners.

While Amaziah fought in Edom, the angry northern troops he had dismissed raided towns across Judah. They killed three thousand people and looted a great deal of property. Compromising with ungodly alliances often brings painful fallout even after those alliances are ended.

After defeating Edom, Amaziah brought their idols back to Jerusalem, set them up as his own gods, and bowed down to burn incense to them. Instead of thanking the Lord for his victory, he foolishly adopted the gods of the very people he had just crushed.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest this account was added by the Chronicler to supply a theological explanation for Amaziah's subsequent military disaster against Israel.

notes.meaning: The Lord was very angry with Amaziah's idolatry, but He mercifully sent a prophet to challenge the king's thinking. The prophet pointed out the obvious foolishness of worshipping gods that could not even rescue their own people.

Amaziah cut the prophet off and angrily asked if anyone had hired him as the king's advisor, threatening to have him killed. The prophet stopped speaking to him, but warned that God had decided to destroy the king because he ignored divine correction. Refusing God's warnings closes the door on mercy.

Amaziah asked for advice from his royal advisors rather than seeking God or the prophet. Emboldened by his recent win against Edom and angry about the border raids, he sent a challenge to King Jehoash of Israel to face him in battle.

Jehoash answered with a fable about a small thorn bush that asked a mighty cedar tree for a marriage alliance, only to be trampled by a wild beast. Jehoash told Amaziah that defeating Edom had made him arrogant and boastful. He warned him to stay home rather than stir up trouble that would ruin both him and Judah.

Amaziah refused to back down from the challenge. This stubbornness came from the Lord, who allowed Amaziah's foolish pride to drive him forward so Judah would be judged for worshipping the Edomite gods.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Traditional Catholic commentators emphasize that God did not force Amaziah to sin, but judicially permitted his heart to harden and follow bad counsel because of his earlier idolatry.

notes.meaning: Jehoash brought his army south, and the two kings clashed at Beth-shemesh in Judah's territory. Judah's army was thoroughly routed by Israel, and every soldier fled back to his home in defeat.

Jehoash captured Amaziah at Beth-shemesh and marched him back to his own capital in Jerusalem. To humiliate Judah and leave Jerusalem defenseless, Jehoash tore down about six hundred feet of the city wall from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate.

Jehoash stripped the temple of all its gold and silver items kept under the care of the family of Obed-edom, and he emptied the royal palace treasury. He also took hostages to guarantee Judah's submission before returning to Samaria.
Amaziah lived for fifteen years after King Jehoash of Israel died. His later years were likely lived in shame and weakened authority, with his son Uzziah sharing power to manage the kingdom.
The writer reminds readers that the full story of Amaziah's deeds, from start to finish, was recorded in the official royal annals of the kings of Judah and Israel.

After Amaziah turned away from the Lord, people in Jerusalem plotted against him. The king fled to the fortified city of Lachish for protection, but the conspirators sent men after him and killed him there.
The king's body was brought back to Jerusalem on horses by those who killed him. He was buried alongside his royal ancestors in the City of David.
